questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Sangam literature primarily provides information about the ancient history of which region?
questions.explanation: Sangam literature is a body of classical Tamil literature that provides valuable information about the social, political and economic life of ancient Tamil-speaking South India.
questions.concept: Sangam Age and literary sources of ancient Indian history.
questions.tip: Associate specific literary corpora with their regions: Sangam literature → Tamil region; Vedic literature → North India.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The 'Din-i-Ilahi' religious order was founded by which Mughal emperor?
questions.explanation: Akbar founded the 'Din-i-Ilahi' (Religion of God) in 1582, attempting to combine elements of several faiths practiced in his empire.
questions.concept: Religious policies of the Mughal emperors.
questions.tip: Akbar's religious policy (Sulh-i-kul, Din-i-Ilahi) is a frequently tested UPSC topic on Mughal administration.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Non-Cooperation Movement was called off by Mahatma Gandhi mainly due to which incident?
questions.explanation: Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922 after the Chauri Chaura incident, where a violent mob clash with police led to deaths, going against his principle of non-violence.
questions.concept: Key turning points of the Indian freedom struggle.
questions.tip: Remember the sequence: Non-Cooperation Movement (1920) → Chauri Chaura (1922) → movement withdrawn.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The French Revolution began in which year?
questions.explanation: The French Revolution began in 1789, triggered by financial crisis, social inequality and Enlightenment ideas.
questions.concept: Major dates in world history.
questions.tip: 1789 is a key anchor date — many related events (Storming of the Bastille, Declaration of the Rights of Man) are dated relative to it.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The 'Treaty of Versailles' (1919), which officially ended World War I, is often cited as a contributing cause of which later conflict?
questions.explanation: The harsh terms imposed on Germany by the Treaty of Versailles created economic hardship and resentment, which many historians cite as a contributing factor to the rise of Nazism and eventually World War II.
questions.concept: Causal links between major 20th-century conflicts.
questions.tip: For 'cause and consequence' questions, look for the treaty/event immediately preceding the conflict in question.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which layer of the Earth's atmosphere contains the ozone layer?
questions.explanation: The ozone layer, which absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, is located in the stratosphere.
questions.concept: Layers of the Earth's atmosphere.
questions.tip: Remember the order from Earth's surface outward: Troposphere, Stratosphere (ozone layer), Mesosphere, Thermosphere, Exosphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which type of rock is formed by the cooling and solidification of molten magma or lava?
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks form when molten magma (below the surface) or lava (above the surface) cools and solidifies.
questions.concept: The rock cycle and rock classification.
questions.tip: Remember: Igneous = cooled magma/lava; Sedimentary = compressed sediments; Metamorphic = transformed by heat/pressure.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Thar Desert is primarily located in which Indian state?
questions.explanation: The Thar Desert, also known as the Great Indian Desert, lies mainly in the state of Rajasthan.
questions.concept: Major physical/geographical features of India and their locations.
questions.tip: Pair India's major deserts, plateaus, and mountain ranges with their primary states for quick recall.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which Indian state has the longest coastline?
questions.explanation: Gujarat has the longest coastline among Indian states, stretching along the Arabian Sea.
questions.concept: Comparative geographical facts about Indian states.
questions.tip: Gujarat's coastline (~1,600 km) is a commonly tested UPSC fact — know the top 2-3 states by coastline length.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Western Ghats are recognised as a biodiversity hotspot primarily because of which characteristic?
options: High endemism and species richness under threat
Being the youngest mountain range in India
Having the highest peak in India
questions.explanation: The Western Ghats are classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and biodiversity hotspot due to their exceptionally high levels of endemic species (found nowhere else) facing habitat loss.
questions.concept: Criteria for classifying a region as a biodiversity hotspot.
questions.tip: A biodiversity hotspot needs both high endemism AND significant habitat loss/threat — having unique species alone is not sufficient.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which is the longest river in the world?
questions.explanation: The Nile River in Africa is traditionally considered the longest river in the world, at approximately 6,650 km (though some studies argue the Amazon may be comparable or longer).
questions.concept: Major world rivers and their lengths.
questions.tip: Know the top rivers by length (Nile, Amazon, Yangtze) — exam answer keys generally follow the traditional Nile-as-longest convention.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Sahara, the world's largest hot desert, is located primarily on which continent?
questions.explanation: The Sahara Desert spans most of North Africa and is the largest hot desert in the world.
questions.concept: Major deserts of the world and their continents.
questions.tip: Distinguish 'largest hot desert' (Sahara, Africa) from 'largest desert overall' (Antarctic Desert, a cold desert).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures:
options: Total income earned by a country's citizens anywhere in the world
The total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period
Only the industrial output of a country
The total exports minus imports of a country
questions.explanation: GDP is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's geographical boundaries during a specific period, regardless of who owns the production.
questions.concept: Definition and scope of GDP as an economic indicator.
questions.tip: GDP = production within borders (territory-based); GNP = production by a country's citizens/residents (nationality-based), wherever located.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Inflation refers to a sustained increase in:
options: The general price level of goods and services
questions.explanation: Inflation is defined as a sustained, general rise in the price level of goods and services in an economy over time, reducing the purchasing power of money.
questions.concept: Definition of inflation.
questions.tip: Don't confuse inflation (general price rise) with a price increase in just one or two goods — it must be broad-based and sustained.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: India's Five-Year Plans were modelled on the planning approach of which country?
questions.explanation: India's Five-Year Plans, introduced from 1951 under the Planning Commission, were influenced by the centralised economic planning model of the Soviet Union.
questions.concept: Historical background of India's planned economic development.
questions.tip: India's Five-Year Plans ended in 2017, replaced by NITI Aayog's more flexible, market-friendly planning approach.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The 'Green Revolution' in India primarily led to a significant increase in the production of which crop?
questions.explanation: The Green Revolution, beginning in the mid-1960s, significantly boosted wheat (and later rice) production through high-yielding seed varieties, irrigation, and fertilizers.
questions.concept: Key agricultural reforms in Indian economic history.
questions.tip: Green Revolution = wheat/rice via high-yield seeds; White Revolution = milk (Operation Flood); Blue Revolution = fisheries.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The Reserve Bank of India uses the 'Repo Rate' primarily to:
options: Control inflation and liquidity in the economy
Fix the exchange rate of the rupee
questions.explanation: The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks; raising or lowering it is a key tool to control inflation and liquidity in the economy.
questions.concept: Monetary policy tools of the RBI.
questions.tip: Higher repo rate → costlier borrowing → less money supply → helps control inflation, and vice versa.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A 'Non-Performing Asset' (NPA) in banking refers to:
options: A loan or advance where interest or principal payment has remained overdue for a specified period
questions.explanation: An NPA is a loan or advance for which the principal or interest payment remained overdue for a period specified by the regulator (typically 90 days in India), signalling credit risk for the bank.
questions.concept: Definition and significance of Non-Performing Assets.
questions.tip: NPAs are a key indicator of a bank's financial health — a rising NPA ratio signals growing credit risk in the banking system.

questions.subject: Environment
questions.text: In a food chain, organisms that manufacture their own food through photosynthesis are called:
questions.explanation: Producers (mainly green plants and algae) manufacture their own food using sunlight through photosynthesis, forming the base of the food chain.
questions.concept: Trophic levels in an ecosystem.
questions.tip: Trophic order: Producers → Primary consumers (herbivores) → Secondary consumers (carnivores) → Decomposers (break down dead matter).

questions.subject: Environment
questions.text: The term 'keystone species' refers to a species that:
options: Is the most abundant species in an ecosystem
Has a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem relative to its abundance
Is found only in marine ecosystems
questions.explanation: A keystone species has an ecological impact disproportionate to its population size — its removal can dramatically alter or collapse the ecosystem structure.
questions.concept: Ecological role of keystone species.
questions.tip: A keystone species need not be abundant or dominant — its importance lies in the structural role it plays, like a keystone in an arch.

questions.subject: Environment
questions.text: Which gas is considered the largest contributor to human-caused (anthropogenic) long-term global warming?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide (CO2), mainly from burning fossil fuels and deforestation, is the largest contributor to anthropogenic global warming due to the sheer volume emitted.
questions.concept: Major greenhouse gases and their relative contribution to warming.
questions.tip: CO2 contributes most by total volume; methane is more potent per molecule but emitted in smaller quantities, with a shorter atmospheric lifetime.

questions.subject: Environment
questions.text: The Paris Agreement (2015) primarily aims to limit global temperature rise to well below:
questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement aims to limit global warming to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, with efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.
questions.concept: Key targets of the Paris Climate Agreement.
questions.tip: Remember the two benchmarks: 'well below 2°C' is the main goal, with 1.5°C as the more ambitious aspirational target.

questions.subject: Environment
questions.text: The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) was adopted at which international summit?
questions.explanation: The Convention on Biological Diversity was opened for signature at the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (Rio Earth Summit) in 1992.
questions.concept: Major international environmental conventions and their origins.
questions.tip: Rio 1992 produced three major conventions: CBD (Biodiversity), UNFCCC (Climate Change), and UNCCD (Desertification).

questions.subject: Environment
questions.text: A protected area where human habitation is allowed along with wildlife conservation, unlike a national park, is called a:
questions.explanation: In a wildlife sanctuary, limited human activities (like grazing, collection of forest produce) may be permitted under regulation, unlike a national park where such activities are generally prohibited.
questions.concept: Categories of protected areas in India.
questions.tip: National Park = strictest protection, no human activity; Wildlife Sanctuary = some regulated human activity allowed; Biosphere Reserve = core + buffer + transition zones.

questions.subject: Environment
questions.text: 'Project Tiger', launched in 1973, was primarily aimed at:
options: Conserving tigers and their habitat through a network of protected tiger reserves
questions.explanation: Project Tiger was launched by the Government of India in 1973 to ensure a viable population of tigers in their natural habitats by establishing dedicated tiger reserves.
questions.concept: Major wildlife conservation projects in India.
questions.tip: Know the launch year and core objective of flagship projects: Project Tiger (1973), Project Elephant (1992).

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.text: The Constitution of India was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on which date?
questions.explanation: The Constitution of India was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949, though it came into effect on 26 January 1950.
questions.concept: Key dates in the making of the Indian Constitution.
questions.tip: Remember: 26 November 1949 = adopted (celebrated as Constitution Day); 26 January 1950 = came into force (Republic Day).

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.text: The 'G20' is a forum primarily comprising:
options: The world's major developed and developing economies
questions.explanation: The G20 is an international forum of the world's major developed and developing economies, representing around 85% of global GDP.
questions.concept: Role and composition of the G20.
questions.tip: The G20 focuses on international economic cooperation and includes both advanced economies (like the US, Germany) and major emerging economies (like India, Brazil).

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.text: Which organ in the human body produces insulin?
questions.explanation: The pancreas produces insulin, a hormone that regulates blood glucose levels.
questions.concept: Basic human physiology and endocrine organs.
questions.tip: Pair key hormones with their producing glands: insulin→pancreas, thyroxine→thyroid, adrenaline→adrenal glands.

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.text: The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) is headquartered in which city?
questions.explanation: ISRO's headquarters is located in Bengaluru, Karnataka, though it has several centres across India including Thiruvananthapuram and Sriharikota.
questions.concept: Key Indian scientific/space organisations and their locations.
questions.tip: ISRO HQ = Bengaluru; Satish Dhawan Space Centre (launch site) = Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh — these are often confused.

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.text: The 'Pulitzer Prize' is primarily awarded in which fields?
questions.explanation: The Pulitzer Prize, awarded in the United States, honours achievements in journalism, literature, and musical composition.
questions.concept: Major international awards and their fields.
questions.tip: Don't confuse the Pulitzer (journalism/literature, US-based) with the Nobel Prize (broader international fields including Peace and Sciences).

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.text: The book 'India Wins Freedom' was authored by:
questions.explanation: 'India Wins Freedom' is an autobiographical account written by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, reflecting on the events leading to India's independence and partition.
questions.concept: Authors of notable books on India's freedom struggle.
questions.tip: Static GK often links freedom movement leaders to their autobiographical works — keep a quick revision list of book-author pairs.

questions.subject: General Awareness
questions.text: International Yoga Day is observed globally on which date?
questions.explanation: International Yoga Day is observed on 21 June every year, following a UN resolution adopted in 2014 on India's proposal.
questions.concept: Important international observance days linked to India.
questions.tip: 21 June was chosen as it is the Summer Solstice, the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere.
